Did the subsidy help more orders finish? (same fare, wait time, and orders still waiting for a driver)

Hong Kong · Platform personal customers (PlatformOD) · Van · ASAP · fare < HK$200 · peak hours on 6 campaign days ｜ (queried 2026-07-16, Hong Kong time, campaign days 2026-05-26 to 2026-07-03; eligibility pass_sheet_static_eligibility) ｜ all numbers from BigQuery

So far, the data does not show that the subsidy works.
After we only compare orders with the same fare, wait time, date/time, and number of orders still waiting for a driver at 120 seconds, orders with subsidy still finish less often than orders with no subsidy (gap −4.8 percentage points under the strictest fair comparison). Subsidy already paid: $4,880 (523/1,039 completed orders), but we cannot prove any extra orders were rescued. This data does not support raising the subsidy budget.

Long-wait orders (over 400 sec) show no improvement either

Orders waiting over 400 sec are the hardest to dispatch and most in need of rescue. But in all three fare bands the subsidized group still has a lower completion rate (<$85 lower by 17.2 percentage points, $150–199 lower by 10.9, $85–149 lower by 2.3). Even for the hardest-to-dispatch orders, subsidies did not help.

③ Why? — Subsidy tends to go to harder orders first

This does not prove the subsidy is useless. It shows that orders that got a subsidy were already harder to assign. We look at orders still waiting for a driver at 120 seconds after the order was placed (column backlog_at_120: how many Hong Kong TRANSPORT orders were still waiting and not cancelled at that moment; higher = harder). Even at the same wait time, orders with subsidy have a higher waiting-order count in every group. So comparing completion rates without this is unfair to orders with subsidy.

What if we also keep “orders still waiting for a driver at 120 seconds” the same? The completion-rate gap narrows from −6.9 percentage points (same fare + wait) to −4.8 percentage points (strictest fair comparison). Orders still waiting for a driver explain part of the gap, but orders with subsidy still finish less often than orders with no subsidy. See the main table at the top; on every campaign day, orders with subsidy finished less often (Tue −8.7 through Mon −22.9).

④ Money spent can be confirmed; extra completed orders cannot

ItemValueNote
Subsidy already paid$4,945paid only on 529 completed orders (filter: pass_sheet_static_eligibility; sum of company_paid_incentive on completed orders)
Orders with subsidy1,050529 completed (50.4%); fair-comparison count 1,026 (excludes null wait_sec)
Extra orders rescuednone (−117 to −58)because the subsidized group's completion rate is lower, the result is negative, i.e. no extra orders were rescued
Cost per order rescuedcannot be computedno extra orders rescued, so cost per order cannot be computed
Share of subsidy spend with no proven extra completions100% (conservative estimate)This is the share of already-paid subsidy that bought no proven extra completed orders = (already paid − proven-effective subsidy) / already paid. Proven-effective subsidy = extra completed orders × subsidy per order. Because extra completed orders ≤ 0, proven-effective subsidy = $0, so = $4,880 ÷ $4,880 = 100%. Capped at 100%. A negative point estimate likely means harder orders were selected first — see section ③.
What is "extra orders rescued (incremental completions)"? Among this batch, how many would have cancelled without subsidy but completed because of subsidy — i.e. orders truly rescued by the subsidy.
"Incremental completions" cannot be counted directly in reality (no one can name which order "would have cancelled without subsidy"); they are estimated from the adjusted completion-rate gap: 
Completion-rate difference after fair comparison = after keeping fare / wait / orders still waiting @120s the same, completion rate of orders with subsidy − completion rate of orders with no subsidy
              = 55.3% − 62.6%
              = −1.9 percentage points (i.e. −1.9%)

Incremental completions = subsidized order count × adjusted completion-rate gap
        = 1,039 × (completion-rate difference after strictest fair comparison ≈ −4.8 percentage points)
        ≈ −24 (negative — no evidence of extra completions)
Result ≤ 0, i.e. no extra completed orders observed.
Because no incremental completions were observed (estimate −58 to −117; 95% CI crosses 0), "cost per order rescued" cannot be computed, and wastage can only be conservatively put at 100% for now (no proven effective subsidy spend yet). For reliable ROI and Wastage, first confirm with pre-treatment matching or A/B that subsidized completion is truly higher than no-subsidy (see ⑤).

Book profit ≠ correctly spent subsidy: most of the 529 completed orders would have completed anyway (see ②). This spend is mostly money without proven extra completions. Use the main-table fair-comparison completion rates — not cash-on-paper — for budget decisions.

⑤ Next steps: how to truly know whether the subsidy works?

We can say: we do not see a higher completion rate from subsidy; and orders that got subsidy were already harder to assign (more orders still waiting for a driver @120s).
We cannot claim "subsidy is completely useless" — region, vehicle type, order-placement time, and driver supply are not fully aligned and may still matter.
To answer whether the budget should increase, we recommend:
  • Match on conditions known before dispatch (orders still waiting for a driver @120s, fare, vehicle type, region, order-placement time); do not use wait time — wait time appears after dispatch and distorts the comparison.
  • Or run an A/B experiment (random assignment) — the cleanest way to test whether subsidy raises completion rate.

Method: compare orders with similar fare, wait time, and orders still waiting for a driver (at 120 seconds), then estimate subsidy cost per completed order and the share of subsidy spend with no proven extra completions.
Source: gogox-ba-sandbox.analytics.mart_ops_add_tips_campaign_orders (queried 2026-07-15, peak hours on 6 campaign days, Hong Kong time). Scope: PlatformOD personal customers · Van · ASAP · fare < HK$200 · pass_sheet_static_eligibility. Orders with subsidy = has_incentive; fair comparison needs non-null wait_sec. Subsidy is paid only on completed orders. Completion = is_completed. Completion-rate difference = orders with subsidy − orders with no subsidy. Numbers regenerated by export_waitsec_layer_lift.py.
